content_preview.title: FDA Approves Sanofi's Sarclisa Escena as First Anticancer Drug Delivered via Wearable On-Body Injector
content_preview.summary: The FDA cleared a subcutaneous, wearable-device formulation of Sanofi's multiple myeloma drug Sarclisa, the first cancer therapy approved for on-body injector delivery.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a subcutaneous formulation of Sanofi's multiple myeloma drug Sarclisa on July 9, 2026, clearing isatuximab-irfc, marketed as Sarclisa Escena, for delivery through a wearable on-body injector, according to the [FDA](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-information-approved-drugs/fda-approves-isatuximab-irfc-subcutaneous-injection-multiple-myeloma-indications). Sanofi announced the approval a day later, calling it the first anticancer trea...

recommendations: Consider adding pharmexec.com and drugdeliverybusiness.com to config/source_allowlist.txt — both are established pharma/medtech trade press with named bylines, editorial standards, and were independently verified to corroborate every claim in this article.

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured 970-word News piece (within the 400-1200 word range for News) with Overview, What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Analysis sections. The What We Don't Know section honestly flags that neither FDA nor Sanofi has disclosed an exact injection-time figure, pricing, or rollout timeline, and raises open questions about adoption pace — this matches what the sources actually omit, not a padding exercise.
editor_notes.source_verification: All four sources fetched successfully (HTTP 200) and sha256-verified against the manifest; I decompressed and read each snapshot in full. source-0.html.gz (fda.gov): confirmed the July 9, 2026 approval date, isatuximab-irfc/Sarclisa Escena naming, all three combination regimens verbatim (Pd for ≥1 prior line incl. lenalidomide+PI; Kd for 1-3 prior lines R/R; VRd for transplant-ineligible NDMM), 1,400 mg dose, CirCLIQ OBDS + manual syringe/infusion-set delivery options, orphan drug designation, IRAKLIA (NCT05405166) 531-patient randomization and ORR figures (71.1%/70.5%), IZALCO (NCT05704049) 74-patient/79.7% ORR, and IsaSocut (NCT05889221) 74-patient/97.3% ORR. source-1.html.gz (Sanofi press release, globenewswire.com, on allowlist): confirmed the Cincinnati-based Enable Injections attribution, enFuse platform, retractable 30g needle spec, exact ORR patient counts (187/263 vs 189/268), relative risk 1.008 with 95% CI 0.903-1.126, systemic administration reaction rates (25% IV vs 1.5% SC), injection site reaction rate (0.4%, 19/5,145 injections, nearly all grade 1 except one grade 2), the five most common adverse reactions (URI, fatigue, pneumonia, musculoskeletal pain, diarrhea), verbatim quotes from Sikander Ailawadhi, Manuela Buxo, and Donna D. Catamero, the ~60-country/four-indication/70,000-patient figures, EU/UK approval, and Japan's manual-injection approval with the OBI submission still under review. source-2.html.gz (pharmexec.com, not on allowlist) and source-3.html.gz (drugdeliverybusiness.com, not on allowlist): both independently corroborate the clinical figures, device specs, and all three quotes with no discrepancies; drugdeliverybusiness.com additionally confirms the Cincinnati HQ and enFuse/CirCLIQ relationship. No claim in the article is unsupported by at least one, and typically two or three, of the four snapshots. No hallucinated quotes, no fabricated specifics, no misattribution found.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every number in the article (dose, patient counts, ORR percentages, relative risk, confidence interval, reaction rates, injection counts, country/patient totals) traces exactly to the FDA and/or Sanofi snapshots. No discrepancies found between the article and any of the four sources.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and clinical throughout; frames the device's benefits with attribution to the company and named clinicians rather than asserting them editorially. The Analysis section appropriately hedges on real-world adoption ('will likely depend on factors the current sources do not address') rather than predicting outcomes.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/2026-07/ and grepped all articles for 'sarclisa', 'sanofi', and 'isatuximab' — no prior or concurrent coverage of this approval. A June 2026 Sanofi/Owkin article and several other FDA-approval articles (EchoNext, Tregzi, Casgevy, Absentia Labs) exist but cover unrelated drugs/companies. This is a genuinely new topic.
concerns: Two of the four cited sources (pharmexec.com, drugdeliverybusiness.com) are not yet in config/source_allowlist.txt. Both were manually verified as credible, bylined pharma/medtech trade publications (MJH Life Sciences and WTWH Media respectively) and their content matches the article claims exactly, so this is treated as an administrative gap rather than an editorial defect — consistent with the 2026-05-28 Inqovi/AML review, which reached the same conclusion for pharmexec.com under the same circumstances.
recommendations: Add pharmexec.com and drugdeliverybusiness.com to config/source_allowlist.txt so future submissions citing these established trade outlets do not trigger this warning.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Clean, well-sourced, appropriately hedged News article. All four sources personally read from disk snapshots and cross-verified against each other with no discrepancies. Verdict upgraded from the script's auto-suggested APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS to APPROVE because the sole finding is an allowlist-configuration gap, not a factual or attribution problem a reader-facing correction could meaningfully address.
